title: Transforms
text:
import torch, numpy as np
from soilspectfm.preprocessing import SNV

SNV (standard normal variate) centers each spectrum on its own mean and divides it by its own standard deviation across wavenumbers. BatchSNV applies SNV as a fastai batch transform, on the device that holds the batch. It uses no fitted statistics. The result for a spectrum depends only on that spectrum, whatever the batch or the train/test split.
A CNN’s default weight initialization, and fastai’s ActivationStats diagnostics, assume inputs of roughly unit scale. BatchSNV also restores that scale after preprocessing for classical models. For example, SNV followed by a Savitzky-Golay derivative leaves spectra with very small values, because the derivative shrinks the unit variance that SNV gives. That scale suits PLSR or a random forest, but not a CNN.


source

BatchSNV
def BatchSNV(
    eps:float=1e-06
):
Center and scale each spectrum by its own mean and standard deviation (SNV)


Spectra with a standard deviation of 0.02 come out with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1:

x = TensorSpectrum(torch.randn(32, 1, 657) * 0.02)
out = BatchSNV()(x)
assert out.mean(-1).abs().max() < 1e-5
assert (out.std(-1, unbiased=False) - 1).abs().max() < 1e-3
float(out.mean(-1).abs().max()), float(out.std(-1, unbiased=False).min()), float(out.std(-1, unbiased=False).max())

(2.1773386649215354e-08, 0.9999467134475708, 0.9999530911445618)


BatchSNV divides by the population standard deviation, as NumPy’s np.std does. It gives the same result as SNV from soilspectfm, which applies SNV to NumPy arrays. The remaining difference comes from eps, which is 1e-6 here and 1e-10 in soilspectfm:

expected = SNV().fit_transform(x.squeeze(1).numpy().astype(float))
test_close(out.squeeze(1).numpy(), expected, eps=1e-3)
np.abs(out.squeeze(1).numpy() - expected).max()

np.float64(0.00018637861981440906)

title: Learner
text:
from fastcore.test import *
from fastai.callback.schedule import *
from soilspecdl.datasets import load_toy_kssl
from soilspecdl.models import SpectralCNN
from soilspecdl.transforms import BatchSNV
A spectral model has two parts. The backbone turns each spectrum into a vector of features. The head maps those features to the prediction. SpectralCNN and its configurations, such as MirzaiCNN, follow this layout.
Fine-tuning a pretrained backbone treats the two parts differently. The head is new and trains first, while the backbone stays fixed. The backbone then adapts with a lower learning rate. fastai does both through parameter groups: Learner.freeze freezes every group except the last, and a slice of learning rates spreads them across the groups, lowest first. fastai’s default Learner puts all parameters in one group, so it can do neither.
source

spectral_splitter
def spectral_splitter(
    m, # Model with `backbone` and `head` attributes
)->list: # Parameter groups: backbone, then head
Split a spectral model’s parameters into backbone and head groups
For the default SpectralCNN, the head holds the 257 parameters of Linear(256, 1). The backbone holds the rest:
model = SpectralCNN()
groups = spectral_splitter(model)
n_params = [sum(p.numel() for p in g) for g in groups]
test_eq(n_params[1], 257)
n_params

[131600, 257]
spectral_learner builds a Learner with spectral_splitter. Its defaults suit regression: mean squared error as the loss and R² as the metric. Pass loss_func and metrics for other tasks, such as classification.
source

spectral_learner
def spectral_learner(
    dls, # DataLoaders, e.g. from `get_spectral_dls`
    model, # Model with `backbone` and `head`, e.g. `SpectralCNN()`
    loss_func:NoneType=None, # Loss function; `MSELossFlat()` if None
    metrics:NoneType=None, # Metrics; `R2Score()` if None
    splitter:function=spectral_splitter, # Function splitting the model's parameters into groups
    *, opt_func:fastai.optimizer.Optimizer | fastai.optimizer.OptimWrapper=Adam, # Optimization function for training
    lr:float | slice=0.001, # Default learning rate
    cbs:fastai.callback.core.Callback | collections.abc.MutableSequence | None=None, # `Callback`s to add to `Learner`
    path:str | pathlib.Path | None=None, # Parent directory to save, load, and export models. Defaults to `dls` `path`
    model_dir:str | pathlib.Path='models', # Subdirectory to save and load models
    wd:float | int | None=None, # Default weight decay
    wd_bn_bias:bool=False, # Apply weight decay to normalization and bias parameters
    train_bn:bool=True, # Train frozen normalization layers
    moms:tuple=(0.95, 0.85, 0.95), # Default momentum for schedulers
    default_cbs:bool=True, # Include default `Callback`s
)->fastai.learner.Learner:
Learner for a spectral model, with backbone and head parameter groups
The examples train on the toy dataset from soilspecdl.datasets, predicting exchangeable potassium (Kex) from 500 KSSL MIR spectra:
toy = load_toy_kssl()
X, y, ids = toy.xy('k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg')
dls, test_idx = get_spectral_dls(X, y.flatten(), toy.wavenumbers, batch_tfms=[BatchSNV()])
The optimizer has one parameter group for the backbone and one for the head:
learn = spectral_learner(dls, SpectralCNN())
learn.create_opt()
test_eq(len(learn.opt.param_groups), 2)
len(learn.opt.param_groups)

2
freeze stops training of the backbone. Following fastai’s default train_bn=True, the backbone’s normalization layers still train, so the head and the BatchNorm weights are the only trainable parameters:
def n_trainable(m): return sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters() if p.requires_grad)

learn.freeze()
test_eq(n_trainable(learn.model.head), 257)
n_trainable(learn.model.backbone), n_trainable(learn.model.head)

(992, 257)
Train the head first, with the backbone frozen. One epoch at each stage shows the steps, not a trained model:
learn.fit_one_cycle(1, lr_max=1e-3)

title: Learner
text:
Cross-validation
Cross-validation chooses a training schedule, such as the number of epochs, without touching the test set. cross_validate trains one model per fold from get_kfold_splitters, and returns each fold’s losses and metrics after every epoch.
fastai’s Recorder keeps the values of the latest fit call only. A fine-tuning schedule makes two calls: one with the backbone frozen, one after unfreezing. _EpochLog records every epoch across all calls:


source

cross_validate
def cross_validate(
    X, # Spectral data matrix
    y, # Target values
    wns, # Wavenumbers
    model_fn, # Function returning a fresh model, called once per fold
    fit, # Function training a fold's `Learner`
    n_splits:int=5, # Number of folds
    seed:int=42, # Random seed for the fold shuffle
    bs:int=32, # Batch size
    batch_tfms:NoneType=None, # Batch transforms, e.g. [BatchSNV()]
    *, loss_func:NoneType=None, # Loss function; `MSELossFlat()` if None
    metrics:NoneType=None, # Metrics; `R2Score()` if None
    splitter:function=spectral_splitter, # Function splitting the model's parameters into groups
    opt_func:fastai.optimizer.Optimizer | fastai.optimizer.OptimWrapper=Adam, # Optimization function for training
    lr:float | slice=0.001, # Default learning rate
    cbs:fastai.callback.core.Callback | collections.abc.MutableSequence | None=None, # `Callback`s to add to `Learner`
    path:str | pathlib.Path | None=None, # Parent directory to save, load, and export models. Defaults to `dls` `path`
    model_dir:str | pathlib.Path='models', # Subdirectory to save and load models
    wd:float | int | None=None, # Default weight decay
    wd_bn_bias:bool=False, # Apply weight decay to normalization and bias parameters
    train_bn:bool=True, # Train frozen normalization layers
    moms:tuple=(0.95, 0.85, 0.95), # Default momentum for schedulers
    default_cbs:bool=True, # Include default `Callback`s
)->pandas.DataFrame: # One row per fold and epoch
Train one model per fold with fit, returning each fold’s losses and metrics after every epoch


model_fn builds a new model for each fold, so no fold starts from weights trained in another. For fine-tuning, model_fn loads the pretrained backbone. fit holds the whole schedule. This one trains the head for 2 epochs with the backbone frozen, then the whole model for 8 epochs. no_bar and no_logging hide fastai’s progress tables, one per fit call and fold:

def fit(learn):
    with learn.no_bar(), learn.no_logging():
        learn.freeze()
        learn.fit_one_cycle(2, lr_max=1e-3)
        learn.unfreeze()
        learn.fit_one_cycle(8, lr_max=slice(1e-5, 1e-3))

res = cross_validate(X, y.flatten(), toy.wavenumbers, model_fn=SpectralCNN, fit=fit, batch_tfms=[BatchSNV()])
test_eq(len(res), 5 * 10)
test_eq(res.groupby('stage')['epoch'].unique().map(list).tolist(), [[0, 1], list(range(2, 10))])
res.head()

from soilspecdl.datasets import load_toy_kssl

X, y, ids = toy.xy('k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg')

title: DataLoader
text:
Splitters
A splitter takes the spectra X and the targets y, and returns train, validation and test indices. get_ks_splitter uses the Kennard-Stone algorithm, which selects samples by their distances in spectral space:


source

get_ks_splitter
def get_ks_splitter(
    test_size:float=0.1, # Proportion of data to hold out for testing
    valid_size:float=0.1, # Proportion of remaining data after test holdout for validation
)-><built-in function callable>: # Function splitting (X,y) into train/valid/test idxs
Create a Kennard-Stone splitter returning train, validation and test indices



train_idx, valid_idx, test_idx = get_ks_splitter()(X, y)
test_eq(len(train_idx) + len(valid_idx) + len(test_idx), len(X))
len(train_idx), len(valid_idx), len(test_idx)

(400, 50, 50)


get_splitter shuffles the samples with a fixed seed, then cuts them into train, validation and test sets. The test set takes the samples that train and validation leave:


source

get_splitter
def get_splitter(
    train_pct:float=0.8, # Proportion of data for training
    valid_pct:float=0.1, # Proportion of data for validation
    seed:int=42, # Random seed for reproducibility
)-><built-in function callable>: # Function splitting (X,y) into train/valid/test idxs
Create a random splitter returning train, validation and test indices



train_idx, valid_idx, test_idx = get_splitter()(X, y)
test_eq((len(train_idx), len(valid_idx), len(test_idx)), (400, 50, 50))
len(train_idx), len(valid_idx), len(test_idx)

(400, 50, 50)


Proportions whose sum exceeds 1 leave no valid test set, so get_splitter raises a ValueError as soon as it is created:

expect_fail(lambda: get_splitter(train_pct=0.8, valid_pct=0.5), contains='must not exceed 1')

<contextlib._GeneratorContextManager>




source

get_pre_splitter
def get_pre_splitter(
    n_train, # Number of rows in the existing training set
    valid_pct:float=0.2, # Proportion of training samples for validation
    seed:int=42, # Random seed for reproducibility
)-><built-in function callable>: # Function splitting (X,y) into train/valid/test idxs
Create a splitter for data whose first n_train rows form the training set


get_pre_splitter suits datasets that come already split into train and test sets. Put the training rows first: the first n_train rows become train and validation, and the rest become the test set. With 100 samples and n_train=80, 20% of the training rows go to validation:

train_idx, valid_idx, test_idx = get_pre_splitter(n_train=80)(np.zeros((100, 5)), np.zeros(100))
test_eq(test_idx, np.arange(80, 100))
len(train_idx), len(valid_idx), len(test_idx)

(64, 16, 20)


Cross-validation trains one model per fold. get_kfold_splitters shuffles the samples once with seed, cuts them into n_splits folds and returns one splitter per fold. Splitter i validates on fold i and trains on the other folds. Its test set is empty. Keep test samples out of X before splitting.


source

get_kfold_splitters
def get_kfold_splitters(
    n_splits:int=5, # Number of folds
    seed:int=42, # Random seed for the shuffle
)->list: # One function per fold, splitting (X,y) into train/valid/test idxs
Create one splitter per fold, each returning train and validation indices and an empty test set


With 500 samples and 5 folds, each splitter trains on 400 samples and validates on 100. Every sample is validated exactly once:

splits = [splitter(X, y) for splitter in get_kfold_splitters(n_splits=5)]
valid_idxs = [valid_idx for _, valid_idx, _ in splits]
test_eq(np.sort(np.concatenate(valid_idxs)), np.arange(len(X)))
[(len(train_idx), len(valid_idx), len(test_idx)) for train_idx, valid_idx, test_idx in splits]

[(400, 100, 0), (400, 100, 0), (400, 100, 0), (400, 100, 0), (400, 100, 0)]

title: DataLoader
text:
Data loader
TensorSpectrum holds spectra as a fastai tensor. show plots a spectrum against its wavenumbers, with the wavenumber axis decreasing from left to right, as is usual for infrared spectra:


source

TensorSpectrum
def TensorSpectrum(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Spectra tensor that plots each spectrum against its wavenumbers in wns



TensorSpectrum(X[0], wns=wns)

/Users/franckalbinet/aai-ws/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/fastai/torch_core.py:140: UserWarning: The given NumPy array is not writable, and PyTorch does not support non-writable tensors. This means writing to this tensor will result in undefined behavior. You may want to copy the array to protect its data or make it writable before converting it to a tensor. This type of warning will be suppressed for the rest of this program. (Triggered internally at /Users/runner/work/pytorch/pytorch/torch/csrc/utils/tensor_numpy.cpp:219.)
  t = torch.as_tensor(x, **kwargs)


TensorSpectrum(shape=(1701,))


Each spectrum stores its own wavenumbers in wns. Spectra on different grids can therefore coexist in one session. This example creates an OSSL spectrum (600–4000 cm⁻¹, step 2) and a Fukushima spectrum (685–3965 cm⁻¹, step 5). Tensor operations, batching and indexing keep wns:

ossl_spc = TensorSpectrum(torch.randn(1, 1701), wns=np.arange(600, 4001, 2))
fuku_spc = TensorSpectrum(torch.randn(1, 657), wns=np.arange(685, 3966, 5))
scaled = ossl_spc * 2
test_eq(scaled.wns, ossl_spc.wns)
test_eq(len(fuku_spc.wns), 657)
scaled.wns[[0, -1]], fuku_spc.wns[[0, -1]]

(array([ 600, 4000]), array([ 685, 3965]))


show_batch plots a batch of spectra in a grid, with each sample’s target as its title. fastai calls it from dls.show_batch:
SpectralBlock is the fastai block for spectra. It turns each row of the spectra matrix into a TensorSpectrum that carries the wavenumbers:


source

SpectralBlock
def SpectralBlock(
    wns, # Wavenumbers, attached to each spectrum as `wns`
):
Block turning each spectrum array into a TensorSpectrum carrying wns




source

get_spectral_dls
def get_spectral_dls(
    X, # Spectral data matrix
    y, # Target values
    wns, # Wavenumbers
    splitter:NoneType=None, # Function returning train/valid/test idxs
    bs:int=32, # Batch size
    batch_tfms:NoneType=None, # Batch transforms, e.g. [BatchSNV()]
)->tuple: # (DataLoaders with the grid in `dls.wns`, test set indices)
Create DataLoaders for spectra, with train, validation and test sets


By default, get_spectral_dls splits the samples at random with get_splitter. show_batch plots spectra with their target values as titles:

dls, test_idx = get_spectral_dls(X, y, wns)
dls.show_batch(max_n=6, ncols=3)








Pass splitter to split another way, for example with Kennard-Stone:

dls_ks, test_idx_ks = get_spectral_dls(X, y, wns, splitter=get_ks_splitter())
len(dls_ks.train_ds), len(dls_ks.valid_ds), len(test_idx_ks)

(400, 50, 50)


For cross-validation, build one DataLoaders per fold:

dls_folds = [get_spectral_dls(X, y, wns, splitter=splitter)[0] for splitter in get_kfold_splitters(n_splits=5)]
[(len(d.train_ds), len(d.valid_ds)) for d in dls_folds]

[(400, 100), (400, 100), (400, 100), (400, 100), (400, 100)]


get_spectral_dls checks that wns has one value per column of X. A mismatch raises a ValueError. Here an OSSL grid of 1,701 wavenumbers is passed with 657-column Fukushima-like spectra:

expect_fail(lambda: get_spectral_dls(np.random.rand(20, 657), np.random.rand(20), np.arange(600, 4001, 2)), contains='`wns` has 1701 values')

<contextlib._GeneratorContextManager>


The grid is a property of the dataset, so the DataLoaders stores it once in dls.wns. Code that needs the grid reads it there. Each spectrum also carries a copy, because show_batch receives spectra without their DataLoaders:

fuku_wns = np.arange(685, 3966, 5)
dls_syn, _ = get_spectral_dls(np.random.rand(100, 657), np.random.rand(100), fuku_wns)
test_eq(dls_syn.wns, fuku_wns)
test_eq(dls_syn.one_batch()[0].wns, dls_syn.wns)
dls_syn.wns[[0, -1]]

array([ 685, 3965])

title: Models
text:
A spectrum is a 1D signal, with one value per wavenumber. The models here are 1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) built from fastai’s ConvLayer. They take batches of shape (batch, channels, wavenumbers), usually with one channel.

from fastcore.test import test_eq



source

ConvBlock
def ConvBlock(
    ni, # input channels
    nf, # output channels
    ks:int=3, # kernel size
    stride:int=1, # stride
    pool_sz:int=3, # pooling kernel size
    act_cls:functools.partial=functools.partial(<class 'torch.nn.modules.activation.LeakyReLU'>, negative_slope=0.1), # activation
    norm_type:fastai.layers.NormType=<NormType.Batch: 1>, # normalization, e.g. `NormType.Instance`
):
Convolution, normalization and activation, then average pooling


The convolution keeps the number of positions, and the pooling divides it by pool_sz. With the default pool_sz=3, 64 positions become 21:

x = torch.randn(32, 61, 64)
block = ConvBlock(61, 128)
out = block(x)
test_eq(out.shape, (32, 128, 21))
out.shape

torch.Size([32, 128, 21])




source

FeatureExtractor
def FeatureExtractor(
    in_channel:int=1, # input channels
    nfs:tuple=(16, 32, 64, 128, 256), # output channels of each conv block
    pool_sz:int=3, # pooling kernel size of each block
    act_cls:functools.partial=functools.partial(<class 'torch.nn.modules.activation.LeakyReLU'>, negative_slope=0.1), # activation
    norm_type:fastai.layers.NormType=<NormType.Batch: 1>, # normalization, e.g. `NormType.Instance`
    conv_block_cls:type=ConvBlock, # conv block class
):
Stack of ConvBlocks, one per entry of nfs, pooled to one vector per spectrum


FeatureExtractor averages over the positions left after its last block. Each spectrum becomes one vector of nf features, whatever its length:

fe = FeatureExtractor(in_channel=61)
out = fe(torch.randn(32, 61, 243))
test_eq(out.shape, (32, fe.nf))
out.shape

torch.Size([32, 256])




source

SpectralCNN
def SpectralCNN(
    in_channel:int=1, # input channels
    nfs:tuple=(16, 32, 64, 128, 256), # output channels of each conv block
    pool_sz:int=3, # pooling kernel size of each block
    act_cls:functools.partial=functools.partial(<class 'torch.nn.modules.activation.LeakyReLU'>, negative_slope=0.1), # activation
    norm_type:fastai.layers.NormType=<NormType.Batch: 1>, # normalization, e.g. `NormType.Instance`
    conv_block_cls:Callable=ConvBlock, # conv block class
    is_classifier:bool=False, # if True, apply a sigmoid to output probabilities
    dropout:float=0.4, # dropout rate
):
1D CNN with a FeatureExtractor backbone and a linear head, for regression or binary classification


SpectralCNN returns one value per spectrum. With is_classifier=True, a sigmoid turns that value into a probability between 0 and 1:

model_reg = SpectralCNN()
model_cls = SpectralCNN(is_classifier=True)

x = torch.randn(32, 1, 1701)
pred_reg = model_reg(x)
pred_cls = model_cls(x)

test_eq(pred_reg.shape, (32,))
assert 0 <= pred_cls.min() and pred_cls.max() <= 1
pred_reg.shape, pred_cls.min().item(), pred_cls.max().item()

(torch.Size([32]), 0.38777458667755127, 0.6036885380744934)


MirzaiCNN builds the architecture from Albinet et al. (2022), Prediction of exchangeable potassium in soil through mid-infrared spectroscopy and deep learning: From prediction to explainability, Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture 6, 230–241. It is a SpectralCNN with five BatchNorm blocks and AvgPool1d(3), sized for MIR spectra of about 1,700 wavenumbers.


source

MirzaiCNN
def MirzaiCNN(
    in_channel:int=1, # input channels
    is_classifier:bool=False, # if True, model will output probabilities
    dropout:float=0.4, # dropout rate
)->__main__.SpectralCNN:
SpectralCNN with the architecture of Albinet et al. (2022)


The paper’s model has 131,857 parameters:

mirzai = MirzaiCNN()
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in mirzai.parameters())
test_eq(n_params, 131_857)
n_params

131857

title: Datasets
text:
Building the dataset
This code built soilspecdl/data/toy_kssl_mir.csv.gz from the cached OSSL file. It needs about 12 GB of memory while pandas reads OSSL:

from soilspecdata.all import load_ossl


toy_targets = ['k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg', 'cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg', 'oc_usda.c729_w.pct', 'clay.tot_usda.a334_w.pct']
ossl = load_ossl()
kssl_mir = ossl[ossl['dataset.code_ascii_txt'] == 'KSSL.SSL'].mir()
X, y, ids = kssl_mir.xy(toy_targets)
idx = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(42).choice(len(X), 500, replace=False))
props = pd.DataFrame(y[idx], index=pd.Index(ids[idx], name='id'), columns=toy_targets)
spectra = pd.DataFrame(X[idx].round(4), index=props.index, columns=kssl_mir.wavenumbers)
pd.concat([props, spectra], axis=1).to_csv('../soilspecdl/data/toy_kssl_mir.csv.gz')

title: SoilSpecDL
text:
SoilSpecDL trains deep learning models on soil infrared spectra. It builds fastai DataLoaders from spectra and soil properties, and provides 1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spectra, including the architecture of Albinet et al. (2022). spectral_learner wraps a model in a fastai Learner with separate backbone and head parameter groups for fine-tuning, and training uses fastai’s learning rate finder, one-cycle training and callbacks.
SoilSpecDL follows the fastai philosophy: state-of-the-art deep learning should be accessible to domain scientists, not just to machine learning practitioners. If you are a soil scientist who uses R packages like resemble or prospectr, this package is designed with you in mind. Training a CNN on a large MIR spectral library should take a few lines of code, not a PhD in machine learning.
SoilSpecDL is part of a Python ecosystem for soil spectroscopy:

title: SoilSpecDL
text:
Installation
pip install -U soilspecdl
To install the development version, with nbdev, run this in the project root with uv:
uv sync --extra dev

title: SoilSpecDL
text:
Quick start
from soilspecdl.all import * imports every SoilSpecDL function and class. Each also has its own module, such as soilspecdl.models, for explicit imports. From fastai, the example imports NormType to configure the CNN, and the training schedule for fit_one_cycle and lr_find.
This example predicts exchangeable potassium (Kex) from the MIR spectra of the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL). SoilSpecData gives the spectra and Kex values of every OSSL sample that has both. The first call to load_ossl downloads about 1 GB, and loading needs about 12 GB of memory. The example preprocesses the spectra with standard normal variate (SNV) and a first derivative, and log-transforms Kex, whose distribution is skewed. Then it trains the CNN of Albinet et al. (2022):

import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from soilspecdata.all import *
from soilspectfm.all import *
from fastai.layers import NormType
from fastai.callback.schedule import *
from soilspecdl.all import *


mir = load_ossl().mir()
X, y, ids = mir.xy('k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg')
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('snv', SNV()),
    ('deriv', SavitzkyGolay(deriv=1))])
X_tfm = pipe.fit_transform(X)
y_tfm = np.log1p(y.flatten())

get_spectral_dls splits the samples into train, validation and test sets, and returns the fastai DataLoaders and the test set’s indices. BatchSNV applies SNV again to each batch, after the derivative has shrunk the spectra to very small values. A CNN’s weight initialization expects inputs of roughly unit scale. Each spectrum in a batch plots against its wavenumbers:

dls, test_idx = get_spectral_dls(
    X_tfm, y_tfm, mir.wavenumbers,
    batch_tfms=[BatchSNV()])
dls.show_batch(max_n=6, ncols=3)








SpectralCNN is a general 1D CNN. nfs sets the number of convolution blocks and their channel widths. pool_sz sets how much each block shortens the spectrum. norm_type sets the normalization. The configuration below reproduces the CNN of Albinet et al. (2022), which MirzaiCNN() also returns. It suits MIR spectra of about 1,700 wavenumbers. For shorter spectra, such as 657 wavenumbers at a 5 cm⁻¹ step, use pool_sz=2 and more blocks.
spectral_learner wraps the model in a fastai Learner, with mean squared error as the loss and R² as the metric:

model = SpectralCNN(nfs=(16, 32, 64, 128, 256), pool_sz=3, norm_type=NormType.Batch)
learn = spectral_learner(dls, model)

Find a learning rate, then train:

learn.lr_find()

learn.fit_one_cycle(20, lr_max=1e-3)

title: SoilSpecDL
text:
Upgrading from 0.1.x
Version 0.2.0 changes the API of soilspecdl. To update code written for version 0.1.x:

StandardizeSpectrum() is now BatchSNV(). BatchSNV divides by the population standard deviation, as np.std and soilspectfm’s SNV do. StandardizeSpectrum divided by the sample standard deviation (n - 1).
read_spa and load_spa are now in soilspecdata. Import them with from soilspecdata.readers import read_spa, load_spa, from SoilSpecData 0.2.2 or later.

title: SoilSpecDL
text:
Upgrading from 0.0.x
Version 0.1.0 changes the API of soilspecdl. To update code written for version 0.0.x:

MirzaiCNN is now a function that returns a SpectralCNN. It no longer accepts out_channel or conv_block_cls. Weights saved from version 0.0.x load unchanged.
FeatureExtractor takes the output channels of each block as nfs, instead of out_channel and n_layers. It returns (batch, channels) instead of (batch, channels, 1).
SpectralBlock() is now SpectralBlock(wns).
The TensorSpectrum.wns class attribute is gone. Each spectrum carries its wavenumbers in wns, and get_spectral_dls stores them once in dls.wns.
get_spectral_dls raises a ValueError when wns does not have one value per column of X.
get_splitter raises a ValueError when train_pct + valid_pct exceeds 1. Before, its check could never fail.
get_fuku_cs137, ConvBlockBaseline, RegressionFloatBlock, SpectralTarget, cnt_params, get_mir_k_1k_smp and the soilspecdl.core module are gone. To count a model’s parameters, use fastai’s learn.summary(). For example data, use load_toy_kssl.
SoilSpecDL now requires SoilSpecData 0.2.1 or later, and SoilSpecTfm 0.1.1 or later.
